slides.0.title: Principles of Distillation
slides.0.subtitle: Pot and column stills, heads and tails, strength and cuts
slides.1.title: Why distil
slides.1.highlights.0.title: Alcohol evaporates more readily than water
slides.1.highlights.0.content: When wine is heated the alcohol vaporises first, and the condensed vapour is stronger and more aromatic
slides.1.highlights.1.title: It takes a lot of wine
slides.1.highlights.1.content: Difford's Guide: Cognac takes roughly nine litres of wine to make one litre of eau-de-vie
slides.1.highlights.2.title: The distilling season
slides.1.highlights.2.content: Both Cognac and Armagnac require distillation to finish by 31 March after the harvest (Wine With Seth, alcademics)
slides.1.content: Distillation concentrates rather than creates; the base wine decides the result.
slides.2.title: Pot still distillation (Cognac)
slides.2.highlights.0.title: The Charentais copper pot
slides.2.highlights.0.content: Cognac must be distilled twice in batch Charentais copper pot stills, whose design and dimensions are legally controlled (Wikipedia, Wine With Seth)
slides.2.highlights.1.title: First distillation
slides.2.highlights.1.content: The first distillation (première chauffe) gives brouillis of about 28–32% (Wine With Seth, Difford's Guide)
slides.2.highlights.2.title: Second distillation
slides.2.highlights.2.content: The second (bonne chauffe) keeps only the heart and discards heads and tails; Difford's Guide puts the output at about 70–72%, though sources differ slightly on the exact figure
slides.2.content: Double distillation gives a purer, finer spirit and underpins Cognac's style.
slides.3.title: Column distillation and cuts
slides.3.highlights.0.title: The Alambic Armagnacais
slides.3.highlights.0.content: Over 95% of Armagnac is made in the small continuous alambic armagnacais, with at most 15 plates; double pot distillation is legal but under 5% (alcademics, WSET Level 2 guide)
slides.3.highlights.1.title: Strength off the still
slides.3.highlights.1.content: WSET Level 2 guide: the Armagnac AOC allows 52–72%, with 52–60% typical, so it keeps more congeners than Cognac
slides.3.highlights.2.title: Heads, hearts and tails
slides.3.highlights.2.content: Batch pot distillation lets the distiller cut heads (about 80%) and tails (about 30%); continuous stills have no heads-and-tails cut (Difford's Guide, alcademics)
slides.3.content: Pot stills lean towards finesse and column stills towards character: the start of the two main styles.
